extracted.intended_audience: Citizens of New York and the broader American public evaluating the proposed Constitution (late-18th-century readers and constitutional deliberants)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative criteria and arguments concerning the design and powers of the U.S. Senate (qualifications, mode of appointment, equality of representation, numbers/terms, and election regulation). Focus is on how institutional features promote stability, check faction, and serve national interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to regulate the TIMES, PLACES, and MANNER of elections
rubrics_metrics.description: The national government's authority over the TIMES, the PLACES, the MANNER of elections is appropriate and is expressly limited to those aspects; qualifications of electors and candidates are fixed in the Constitution and are not alterable by the legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The power to set times/places/manner is defensible because it provides uniformity and practical regulation of elections; it does not permit changing the qualifications of voters or candidates. Concerns that this power could be used to create class preference are misplaced unless property qualifications are prescribed — which the national government lacks authority to do. Example wording: 'Its authority would be expressly restricted to the regulation of the TIMES, the PLACES, the MANNER of elections.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity in time of elections
rubrics_metrics.description: Holding federal elections at uniform times across the states is a positive advantage: it can prevent gradual accretion of a prevailing improper spirit, facilitate total dissolution/renewal of the body, and aid regular rotation in the Senate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniform timing reduces contagion of example and successive assimilation of improper spirit; without uniformity elections could be held at many different dates (e.g., March through November), preventing total renewal and enabling gradual, persistent influence. Also aids convenient annual assembly and Senate rotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locality/Place of elections should not be unduly confined
rubrics_metrics.description: Confined places of election (e.g., requiring remote electors to vote in a single city) would likely disenfranchise distant voters and favor local urban interests, making such a restriction objectionable and impractical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confining places of election would discourage remote electors from voting and could produce an unrepresentative body dominated by those near the designated place. The text uses the example of Albany vs. remote counties to illustrate how centralizing place of election reduces participation and biases outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications for senators (age and citizenship requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Senators should be older and longer-tenured citizens than representatives: minimum age thirty and nine years' citizenship (versus twenty-five and seven for representatives), to ensure greater information, stability of character, and reduced susceptibility to foreign influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: the senatorial trust requires maturity, greater information, and stability; nine years is a mediocrity balancing exclusion of adopted citizens and avoiding hasty admission that might open channels for foreign influence. These fixed qualifications serve as safeguards against foreign bias and insufficient experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment of senators by State legislatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing senators by State legislatures is recommended as congenial to public opinion; it favors a select appointment and gives state governments agency in the federal formation, linking state and national systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mode of appointment is commended for its double advantage: selectivity (a 'select appointment') and preserving state influence in national government formation — a political compromise to secure state support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of representation in the Senate (state equality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Equality of representation (each State having the same vote) in the Senate is a compromise between proportional and equal representation suitable for a compound republic; it recognizes residuary sovereignty of states and acts as an impediment to improper legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equality protects smaller states' sovereignty and provides an additional check on lawmaking by requiring concurrence of a majority of people and a majority of states. It is defended as a necessary political compromise rather than a purely theoretical ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate as a double security/check against usurpation
rubrics_metrics.description: A second legislative body (the Senate) provides a salutary check on government by requiring concurrence of two distinct bodies, doubling security against schemes of usurpation, perfidy, or corruption that might succeed in a single assembly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The improbability of sinister combinations increases with dissimilarity between the two bodies; therefore, the Senate should be distinguished by circumstances (size, tenure) that create such dissimilarity while preserving harmony on proper measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate must be less numerous and have greater firmness
rubrics_metrics.description: To correct the propensity of numerous assemblies to yield to sudden passions and factious leaders, the corrective body ought to be less numerous and possess great firmness, which implies longer tenure and select membership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smaller membership and longer terms reduce susceptibility to transient popular passions and facilitate deliberation. This is an anti-pattern against large, frequently-changing bodies incapable of resisting faction-driven intemperance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate should provide legislative knowledge and expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Because many representatives are drawn from private pursuits and serve short terms, they lack sustained ability to study laws and national affairs; a Senate is necessary to supply continuity of knowledge, reduce legislative blunders, and produce more considered legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: numerous repealing/amending laws and defective codes arise from legislative inexperience. The Senate's composition and tenure should remedy the deficiency of sustained legislative learning and coherent long-term policy-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate to provide continuity against mutability of public councils
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent wholesale change in representative bodies produces mutability in policy that harms national character, foreign respect, economic enterprise, and the stability necessary for improvements and investments; the Senate reduces this mutability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stability enhances foreign respect, fosters confidence for commerce and improvements, and preserves reverence for government. The text argues that continual change prevents coherent long-term law and policy, benefiting moneyed few over general public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate to enable responsibility for long-term objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Responsibility is meaningful only when it pertains to objects within the power of the actors and to operations whose results constituents can judge; assemblies with very short terms cannot be held responsible for long-term projects, so a Senate with longer continuity is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short-term assemblies can reasonably be held accountable for immediate operations but not for chains of measures requiring many years; thus, a body of greater permanence is the proper locus of responsibility for extended policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate as a check against popular errors/delusions
rubrics_metrics.description: A temperate and stable Senate can defend the people from their own temporary errors and passions by checking ill-considered measures until reason and truth regain authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In times of popular delusion, the Senate's deliberation can prevent the enactment of laws that the people may later regret. Historical examples (Athens) are invoked to show the perils of unchecked popular impulsiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design features (number and term) should produce institutional dissimilarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of senators and length of their terms should be deliberately chosen to make the Senate dissimilar to the House in genius and temperament, thereby reducing risk of common factional capture and improving the probability of wise counsel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dissimilarity increases the improbability of sinister combinations; thus, the Senate ought to be less numerous and of longer tenure 'consistent with a due harmony in all proper measures.' The choice of numbers/terms is to be judged by the purposes the Senate must serve: stability, experience, and deliberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation composition reflects prevailing state interests, limiting class bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Because state legislatures and local conditions shape federal representation, no assured method exists for securing a preference to 'the wealthy and the well-born' except by altering qualifications; thus fears that election regulation will systematically favor a class are overstated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: landed vs. mercantile bias will be unlikely because composition mirrors state majorities and local variety; any effective class preference would require property qualifications, which federal government lacks authority to impose. This serves as a rebuttal to objections claiming systemic class capture via election regulation.
